interesting, in case the input is going trough we usually don't pipeline the wgmma wait based on this logic: https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/main/lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms/Pipeliner/WGMMAPipeline.cpp#L40

We could move it in the next iteration but then it is hard to make sure the compiler doesn't later moves it across non side-effecting ops

This is not an issue in the triton compiler, AFAIK, but in ptxas. It's an issue known to nvidia, but in their words:
>The compiler team confirms this is a long-standing bug in the compiler's physical register liveness model with no simple fix.

We tried a number of workarounds at a PTX level in triton but all of them were overridden by ptxas.

For OAI reference, the discussion of this bug is in:
https://triton-lang.slack.com/archives/C04CZ1MCL65/p1755081175673579

if triton uses wgmma_wait 3 is it a functional bug in Triton

The problem is that we assume ptxas will schedule the LHS argument update so that instead of updating the LHS registers all in one go, it goes as:
```
wgmma_wait 1
update A[0]
wgmma acc, A[0], B[0]
wgmma_wait 1
update A[1]
wgmma acc, A[1], B[1]
```
I guess the ldmatrix somehow blocks this rescheduling.

It's unclear how we could fix this at an llvm level. You would need to ensure that `A` lives in a different set of logical registers to the LHS argument to the wgmma which requires us to somehow allocate registers in llvm which is nonsense. WGMMA is just broken from a compiler perspective.
Maybe we could create temporary registers in the inline ptx just for the LHS argument, and do manual `mov` instructions?

I believe I had tried adding moves to make the "ptx" correct but that didn't help. 
Let's leave this up to NV engineers who added this pipelining optimizations and own ptxas behavior

> Maybe we could create temporary registers in the inline ptx just for the LHS argument, and do manual `mov` instructions?

If this is the same problem as the one we discussed before (like @lezcano said), Triton does do this trivial mov stuff. But ptxas had a bug which defeated this trick. The issue was fixed internally and should be available in CUDA 13.2.

Ah, sorry for not having fully explained the context. The thing is that when we realised of this issue, we tried always emitting a mov before the `wgmma` instruction, but ptxas would override this decision and still emit incorrect code, so we removed that hack.

According to @masahi 's info, it looks like we should go back to implement that to be sure that, at least on our side, our code is correct, and then whenever the ptxas lands we should be in a good place.
The pseudocode you posted is equivalent, but with 8 splits instead of 2. In your case w[2-8] are still being used while they're being assigned from the split op.

> The pseudocode you posted is equivalent, but with 8 splits instead of 2. In your case w[2-8] are still being used while they're being assigned from the split op.

What do you mean? The overwrite to the registers is not done by the split op, but by `mov` op before each WGMMA ops. At the PTX level, upcast / split are done at the beginning of the loop, but each WGMMA makes sure to do "trivial mov" so that it consumes registers overwritten at the right point. 

But yeah, my pseudocode is a bit confusing, it's just for explaining the structure of the kernel at the high level.  Updated to make `mov` before each WGMMA explicit.
Oh, I saw the comment before you edited it to add the `mov` instructions. Yes I agree that `mov` should theoretically fix it, modulo any `ptxas` bugs.

not a pipeliner issue, we can just always emit the `mov` when lowering the RS WGMMA and that should always give us correctness.

I did some experiments with `ptxas` from CUDA 13.1 (`build cuda_13.1.r13.1/compiler.36836380_0`).

The kernel ([wgmma_register_sync_test.ptx.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25289161/wgmma_register_sync_test.ptx.txt)) doesn't perform a correct matmul, it only intends to investigate the behaviour of `ptxas`'s liveness analysis. It follows the structure of the code in my previous [comment](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/issues/9433#issuecomment-3891954250).

`ptxas` maps `%a0` and `%d0`, `%a1` and `%d1` to the same physical register and then detects its own mistake:
It changes `wait_group` to `0` (`WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE gsb0, 0x0;` in [wgmma_register_sync_test_c7513.sass.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25289353/wgmma_register_sync_test_c7513.sass.txt)) and prints `(C7513) Potential Performance Loss: wgmma.mma_async instructions are serialized due to non wgmma instructions defining input registers of a wgmma between start and end of the pipeline stage in the function 'wgmma_register_sync_test' in line 0`.

So the test does not expose a correctness bug in `ptxas`. With correct code (copy `%d` to `%a` before `fence/mma_async`), it produces correct but slow code. Without the copy, it's simply garbage in, garbage out.

In order to prevent `ptxas` from mapping `%a` and `%d` to the same physical register, I manually extended the lifetime of `%a` until after the `wait_group` with extra `xor %d, %d, %a` instructions. With those, it leaves `wait_group` unchanged (`WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE gsb0, 0x1;` in [wgmma_register_sync_test_xor.sass.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25289704/wgmma_register_sync_test_xor.sass.txt)) and `C7513` goes away.

So I'm wondering, is the `ptxas` fix coming in CUDA 13.2 about correctly analyzing the lifetime of `mma_async` input registers and producing *faster* code, or is there also a correctness bug that I failed to trigger in my experiments?

I did not experiment with register ping-pong and an unrolled loop (second snippet in [this comment](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/issues/9433#issuecomment-3890904677)). I assumed this is the recommended structure to work around the `ptxas` limitation, but I suspect that it would result in the same `C7513`.

> So I'm wondering, is the ptxas fix coming in CUDA 13.2 about correctly analyzing the lifetime of mma_async input registers and producing faster code, or is there also a correctness bug that I failed to trigger in my experiments?

We'll confirm next week whether the kernel compiles with the ptxas fix coming in CUDA 13.2 and emits valid SASS, stay tuned.

> So I'm wondering, is the ptxas fix coming in CUDA 13.2 about correctly analyzing the lifetime of mma_async input registers and producing faster code, or is there also a correctness bug that I failed to trigger in my experiments?

Sorry I haven't fully read your analysis, but the fix coming to CUDA 13.2 is strictly for correctness, not performance. In my  pseudocode below, the positions of movs wrt `wait 7` is crucial for correctness. Triton is emitting correct PTX (race free), and the fix to ptxas will also make the SASS correct. 

```
W_bf16 = upcast W_mxfp4, scales 
w1, w2, ... w8 = split W_bf16 // split into 8 pieces along K dim

mov w1', w1
wgmma w1', x1, acc  // w1 is reg, x1 is smem
commit_group
wait 7

mov w2', w2
wgmma w2', x2, acc
commit_group
wait 7
.
.
.
mov w8', w8
wgmma w8', x8, acc
commit_group
wait 7
```

My repro and experiments show something different.
- Triton emits incorrect PTX without the `mov`.
- With the `mov`, `ptxas` 13.1 emits correct but slow code (`WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE gsb0, 0x0;`).

@chsigg I have an update on this issue. When I said "Triton generates movs", that turned out to be true only for some workloads in the MoE test that I was looking at last year. Moreover, those movs are actually generated by LLVM from `insert / bitcast` etc in https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/main/third_party/nvidia/lib/TritonNVIDIAGPUToLLVM/DotOpToLLVM/WGMMA.cpp#L118-L125. Today I found that there are workloads in the MoE test for which those `insert / bitcast` are optimized away by LLVM which results in

```
LHS = ...

wait N - 1

wgmma acc, LHS, RHS
```  

rather than

```
LHS = ...

wait N - 1

reg = mov LHS
wgmma acc, reg, RHS
```  

According to @ThomasRaoux, such copy propagation across `wait N - 1` by LLVM is legal. So we cannot rely on LLVM to materialize `mov` from `insert / bitcast`. Previously OAI tried such manual `mov` insertion in Triton, but due to the bug in ptxas, such trick didn't work. Now that the fixed ptxas is coming, we should revisit this. I don't know why your workload + manual mov is not affected by the ptxas bug, but it's good that you don't have to wait for the 13.2 update.
When investigating this I added the manual mov emission during wgmma lowering but I removed it since it did not fix the issue. Feel free to submit a PR emitting this
This landed in https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/9514, so I don't think there is much more to do on the triton side of things. @chsigg do you want to keep this open or should we close it?
I think it makes sense to keep it open until a fixed ptxas is released and Triton is updated to use it.

Thanks for adding these `mov`s. I've tested this change at HEAD with my repro from the top.

It looks like the `mov`s are placed after instead of before the `fence`. I've opened https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/9530 to put them before.

With that, the PTX looks correct, but the SASS does have the RAW hazard: `R96` and `R88` (the inputs to the second set of `HGMMA`) are written before the first `WARPGROUP.DEPBAR`: [wgmma_register_sync_repro_kernel.sass.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25444162/wgmma_register_sync_repro_kernel.sass.txt). This is with `ptxas V13.1.115`.

Given that it will likely take a while before XLA upgrades to CUDA 13.2, we will play it safe and use the `wait_group 0` [patch](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/main/third_party/triton/temporary/wgmma_pipeline_fix.patch) for the time being.
I noticed that the issue is now documented at https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-toolkit-release-notes/index.html#id3. Thanks!
Hi @chsigg, 13.3 was posted today. Would you be able to confirm with the latest ptxas that the bug has been resolved?
Yes, I can confirm that the issue is fixed for my repro. The register `MOV`s are staggered around the `DEPBAR` instructions when compiled with ptxas 13.3, but not before.
Great thanks for confirming it's been fixed. @lezcano @ThomasRaoux we can now close this issue
